Antifolates.note: Block dihydrofolate reductase, so DHF isn’t recycled to THF: no new thymidine or purines. Which organism’s DHFR each one prefers decides what it treats.

Thymidylate synthase inhibitors.note: Fluoropyrimidines: 5-FdUMP locks thymidylate synthase with methylene-THF, so no dTMP ("thymineless death"). Leucovorin strengthens the lock; uridine triacetate is the antidote.

DHODH inhibitors.note: Block dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (de novo pyrimidine synthesis), which activated lymphocytes depend on. Hepatotoxic and teratogenic; washed out with cholestyramine.

Thiopurines.note: Purine analogs that shut down de novo purine synthesis at PRPP amidotransferase. Xanthine oxidase and TPMT break them down: allopurinol raises their levels, and low TPMT activity means bone-marrow suppression.

IMP dehydrogenase inhibitors.note: Block IMP dehydrogenase, so cells run short of GMP and GTP; lymphocytes, which rely on de novo purine synthesis, are hit hardest.

Xanthine oxidase inhibitors.note: Block xanthine oxidase, so less uric acid: gout, and preventing tumor lysis syndrome. They raise azathioprine and 6-MP levels.

Statins.note: Block HMG-CoA reductase, so liver cells make more LDL receptors and LDL falls. Myopathy (worse with fibrates and CYP3A4 inhibitors), raised liver enzymes.

Azole antifungals.note: Block fungal lanosterol 14α-demethylase (CYP51), so no ergosterol in the fungal membrane. They inhibit human CYP450s too (drug interactions).

DOPA decarboxylase inhibitors.note: Block DOPA decarboxylase outside the brain (they don’t cross the blood–brain barrier), so more levodopa reaches the brain with less nausea and hypotension.

VMAT inhibitors.note: Block the vesicular monoamine transporter, so monoamines aren’t packed into vesicles and are broken down instead.

HIV protease inhibitors.note: The -navirs. Atazanavir and indinavir also inhibit UGT1A1: a harmless unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia.

5α-Reductase inhibitors.note: Block 5α-reductase, so less testosterone becomes DHT: BPH, male-pattern hair loss. PSA falls by about half.

Aromatase inhibitors.note: Block aromatase, so androgens aren’t turned into estrogens: ER-positive breast cancer after menopause. Bone loss, joint pain.

Glucocorticoids.note: Block phospholipase A₂ (via annexin A1) and cut COX-2 production, so every eicosanoid falls; broadly anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive.

NSAIDs.note: Block cyclooxygenase (COX-1 and COX-2), so fewer prostaglandins and less thromboxane. Gastric ulcers, kidney injury (afferent arteriole), bleeding.

Direct factor Xa inhibitors.note: The -xabans: block factor Xa directly, no antithrombin needed. Oral, no routine monitoring; andexanet alfa reverses them.

Heparins.note: Activate antithrombin, which shuts down factor Xa (and, with unfractionated heparin, thrombin). Safe in pregnancy; heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.

Direct thrombin inhibitors.note: Block thrombin directly, no antithrombin needed. Used when heparin can’t be (HIT).

Thrombolytics.note: Turn plasminogen into plasmin, which dissolves fibrin clots: ischemic stroke, STEMI without PCI, massive PE. Bleeding; contraindicated after recent surgery or hemorrhagic stroke.

Antifibrinolytics.note: Block the lysine binding sites on plasminogen, so it can’t bind fibrin and be activated: bleeding, heavy menstrual bleeding, trauma.

Complement C5 inhibitors.note: Antibodies against C5: no C5 cleavage, so no MAC. PNH, atypical HUS, myasthenia gravis. Vaccinate against Neisseria meningitidis first.

SGLT2 inhibitors.note: The -gliflozins: block SGLT2 in the proximal tubule, so glucose (and sodium) stay in the urine. Type 2 diabetes, heart failure, CKD; genital infections, euglycemic DKA.

Loop diuretics.note: Block NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb, so the medullary gradient is lost: the strongest diuretics. Edema, hypercalcemia; hypokalemia, metabolic alkalosis, ototoxicity, and they make you lose calcium.

Thiazides.note: Block NCC in the distal convoluted tubule. Hypertension, calcium kidney stones, nephrogenic DI; hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hypercalcemia, hyperglycemia, hyperuricemia.

ENaC blockers.note: Potassium-sparing diuretics that block ENaC in the principal cell, so less sodium in and less potassium out. Hyperkalemia.

Vaptans.note: Block the V2 receptor, so no aquaporin-2 goes into the membrane and free water is lost: SIADH, euvolemic hyponatremia. Correct sodium slowly (osmotic demyelination).

ACE inhibitors.note: The -prils: block angiotensin-converting enzyme, so less angiotensin II and aldosterone. The efferent arteriole relaxes, so GFR falls a little (creatinine may rise up to about 30%) and the kidney is protected in diabetic nephropathy. Hyperkalemia; bradykinin builds up: dry cough, angioedema. Not in pregnancy or bilateral renal artery stenosis.

ARBs.note: The -sartans: block the AT1 receptor. The same kidney effects as ACE inhibitors (efferent arteriole relaxes, GFR falls a little, hyperkalemia) without the bradykinin cough. Not in pregnancy.
